help.intro: Family and people words are among the first nouns you need — you introduce your family to new people, and you talk about your Bruder and your Freundin constantly. Learn each one with its article, because here the gender mostly follows the person: der Vater, die Mutter, der Sohn, die Tochter. Two exceptions show that German gender is grammar, not biology: das Kind and das Mädchen are neuter, because -chen words are always das. A pattern worth learning early: many people-words make their female form by adding -in — Freund → Freundin, Lehrer → Lehrerin, Student → Studentin — and the plural of these is -innen.

tips.title: The core family, with articles
tips.text: der Vater, die Mutter, die Eltern (plural only); der Bruder, die Schwester, die Geschwister; der Sohn, die Tochter, das Kind; der Großvater/Opa, die Großmutter/Oma; der Mann, die Frau.

examples.de: Ich habe einen Bruder und eine Schwester.
examples.en: I have a brother and a sister.

examples.de: Meine Eltern wohnen in Wien.
examples.en: My parents live in Vienna.

check.q: ____ Tochter heißt Emma.
check.why: Family words mostly follow the person: a daughter is female, so die Tochter.

visual.caption: Together: die Eltern (parents), die Geschwister (siblings), die Großeltern (grandparents), die Kinder (children).

tips.title: Female forms end in -in
tips.text: der Freund → die Freundin, der Lehrer → die Lehrerin, der Student → die Studentin, der Arzt → die Ärztin (often with an umlaut). Plural: -innen.

examples.de: Anna ist meine Freundin. Sie ist Ärztin.
examples.en: Anna is my friend (female). She is a doctor.

examples.de: Die Lehrerinnen sind nett.
examples.en: The (female) teachers are nice.

check.q: Herr Weber ist Student. Frau Weber ist auch ____.
check.why: Add -in for one woman: Student → Studentin. -innen is the plural.

tips.title: das Mädchen, das Kind
tips.text: A girl is neuter — because -chen makes every noun das. The pronoun is es: Das Mädchen ist klein. Es heißt Mia.

examples.de: Das Kind spielt. Es ist drei Jahre alt.
examples.en: The child is playing. It is three years old.

examples.de: Das Mädchen heißt Mia. Es ist sechs.
examples.en: The girl is called Mia. She is six.

tips.trap: gender is grammatical. A girl being 'it' feels wrong in English and is simply correct in German.

check.q: ____ Mädchen spielt im Garten.
check.why: Every -chen word is neuter, so it is das Mädchen, even though it means a girl.

tips.title: Freund or Freundin — friend or partner?
tips.text: mein Freund / meine Freundin with mein can mean boyfriend / girlfriend. To say just a friend, Germans say ein Freund von mir / eine Freundin von mir.

examples.de: Das ist meine Freundin Lena.
examples.en: This is my girlfriend Lena. (or: my friend Lena — context decides)

examples.de: Tom ist ein Freund von mir.
examples.en: Tom is a friend of mine.

check.q: Tom is just a friend, not your boyfriend. Tom ist ____.
check.why: mein Freund can mean boyfriend; ein Freund von mir clearly means just a friend.

remember: der Vater, die Mutter, das Kind — blue, red, green — the three colours in one family.
Add -in and the man becomes a woman: Freund-in, Lehrer-in, Student-in.

context.de: Das ist meine Familie. Mein Vater heißt Peter und meine Mutter heißt Sabine. Ich habe einen Bruder, Jonas, und eine Schwester, Mia. Mia ist noch ein Kind – sie ist sechs. Meine Oma wohnt auch bei uns. Und das ist Lena, eine Freundin von mir.
context.en: This is my family. My father is called Peter and my mother is called Sabine. I have a brother, Jonas, and a sister, Mia. Mia is still a child – she's six. My grandma lives with us too. And this is Lena, a friend of mine.

mistakes.why: -chen makes a noun neuter, whatever it means.
A female friend takes the -in form.
Eltern is plural only, so its article is die.

help.hook: Vater, Mutter, Bruder, Freundin — the people words you will use every day, each learnt with its der, die or das.

sentences.sentence: Eine Frau mit einem Kind ist ____.
sentences.english: A woman with a child is ____ (the mother).
sentences.why: die Mutter — 'mother'. Family words for women are die; Mutter even breaks the -er rule.

sentences.sentence: Ein Mann mit einem Kind ist ____.
sentences.english: A man with a child is ____ (the father).
sentences.why: der Vater — 'father'. Male family members are der.

sentences.sentence: Jonas ist der Sohn von Mama und Papa. Er ist ____.
sentences.english: Jonas is the son of Mum and Dad. He is ____ (my brother).
sentences.why: der Bruder — 'brother'. A shared set of parents makes brothers and sisters.

sentences.sentence: Mia ist die Tochter von Mama und Papa. Sie ist ____.
sentences.english: Mia is the daughter of Mum and Dad. She is ____ (my sister).
sentences.why: die Schwester — 'sister'; die because she is female.

sentences.sentence: Mama, Papa und ein Junge: Der Junge ist ____.
sentences.english: Mum, Dad and a boy: the boy is ____ (the son).
sentences.why: der Sohn — 'son'; seen from the parents, the boy is their Sohn.

sentences.sentence: Mama, Papa und ein Mädchen: Das Mädchen ist ____.
sentences.english: Mum, Dad and a girl: the girl is ____ (the daughter).
sentences.why: die Tochter — 'daughter'; seen from the parents, the girl is their Tochter.

sentences.sentence: Der Vater von Papa ist ____.
sentences.english: Dad's father is ____ (the grandfather).
sentences.why: Your father's father is der Großvater — literally the 'great-father'; Opa is the cosy word.

sentences.sentence: Die Mutter von Mama ist ____.
sentences.english: Mum's mother is ____ (the grandmother).
sentences.why: Your mother's mother is die Großmutter — 'great-mother'; Oma is the cosy word.

sentences.sentence: Ein Junge oder ein Mädchen ist ____.
sentences.english: A boy or a girl is ____ (a child).
sentences.why: das Kind — 'child'. das, whatever the child's sex: the word's gender is grammatical.

sentences.sentence: Herr Braun hat eine Frau und zwei Kinder. Er ist ein ____ .
sentences.english: Mr Braun has a wife and two children. He is a ____ (man).
sentences.why: der Mann means both 'man' and 'husband' — eine Frau haben = to have a wife.

sentences.sentence: Frau Braun hat einen Mann und zwei Kinder. Sie ist eine ____ .
sentences.english: Mrs Braun has a husband and two children. She is a ____ (woman).
sentences.why: die Frau means both 'woman' and 'wife' — and doubles as 'Mrs' before a name.

sentences.sentence: Tom ist sieben Jahre alt. Er ist ein ____ .
sentences.english: Tom is seven years old. He is a ____ (boy).
sentences.why: der Junge — 'boy'. One of the few masculine words ending in -e.

sentences.sentence: Mia ist sechs Jahre alt. Sie ist ein ____ .
sentences.english: Mia is six years old. She is a ____ (girl).
sentences.why: das Mädchen — 'girl'. -chen words are always das, even for a girl: ein Mädchen.

sentences.sentence: Eltern und Kinder zusammen sind ____.
sentences.english: Parents and children together are ____ (a family).
sentences.why: die Familie — 'family'; an -e word, and like most of them it is die.

sentences.sentence: Tom ist nett. Ich mag Tom. Tom ist ____.
sentences.english: Tom is nice. I like Tom. Tom is ____ (my friend).
sentences.why: der Freund — 'friend' (male). Careful: mein Freund can also mean 'my boyfriend'.

sentences.sentence: Lena ist nett. Ich mag Lena. Lena ist ____.
sentences.english: Lena is nice. I like Lena. Lena is ____ (my friend).
sentences.why: die Freundin — Freund + -in makes it female; meine Freundin can also mean 'my girlfriend'.

sentences.sentence: Ich habe einen Sohn und eine Tochter. Das sind meine ____ .
sentences.english: I have a son and a daughter. They are my ____ (children).
sentences.why: Kinder is the plural of das Kind — one of the -er plurals.

sentences.sentence: Meine Mutter und mein Vater sind meine ____ .
sentences.english: My mother and my father are my ____ (parents).
sentences.why: die Eltern — 'parents'. It only exists in the plural.

sentences.sentence: Mein Bruder und meine Schwester sind meine ____ .
sentences.english: My brother and my sister are my ____ (siblings).
sentences.why: die Geschwister — 'siblings', brothers and sisters together; plural only.

help.intro: Where are you from, what do you speak, what are you — three of the first questions anyone asks, and three answers you will give again and again. Most country names have no article and take aus directly: aus Deutschland, aus Spanien. A handful are feminine or plural and keep their article, which then changes after aus: die Schweiz → aus der Schweiz, die Türkei → aus der Türkei, die USA → aus den USA. Languages are neuter nouns written with a capital (Deutsch, Englisch) and most end in -isch. Nationalities are people-nouns: Deutscher / Deutsche, Engländer / Engländerin, Franzose / Französin — and after sein they take no article: Ich bin Deutsche.

tips.title: aus + country, no article
tips.text: Ich komme aus Deutschland / aus Spanien / aus Japan. Cities work the same way: aus Berlin, aus Wien.

examples.de: Woher kommst du? – Aus Italien, aus Rom.
examples.en: Where are you from? – From Italy, from Rome.

examples.de: Wir kommen aus Deutschland, aus Hamburg.
examples.en: We come from Germany, from Hamburg.

check.q: Lisa kommt ____ Österreich.
check.why: Most countries have no article, so aus goes straight in front: aus Österreich, aus Spanien.

root.q: Does the country take an article?

yes.q: Is it plural (die USA, die Niederlande)?

tips.title: The countries with an article
tips.text: die Schweiz, die Türkei, die Ukraine, die Niederlande (pl.), die USA (pl.). After aus the article changes: aus der Schweiz, aus der Türkei, aus den USA, aus den Niederlanden.

examples.de: Sie kommt aus der Schweiz.
examples.en: She comes from Switzerland.

examples.de: Er kommt aus den USA.
examples.en: He comes from the USA.

tips.trap: the article after aus is the dative (der / den). For now learn these four as fixed phrases; the system behind them comes later in the course.

check.q: Mein Kollege kommt ____ Türkei.
check.why: die Türkei is one of the countries that keeps its article, and after aus die becomes der: aus der Türkei.

tips.title: Languages: capital, -isch, no article
tips.text: Ich spreche Deutsch, Englisch und ein bisschen Französisch. sprechen + language, no article. The adjective is the same word in lowercase: ein deutsches Buch. Some countries have more than one language — in der Schweiz spricht man Deutsch, Französisch, Italienisch und Rätoromanisch; this quiz asks for the one most people speak.

examples.de: In Brasilien spricht man Portugiesisch.
examples.en: In Brazil people speak Portuguese.

examples.de: Sprichst du Spanisch? – Ein bisschen.
examples.en: Do you speak Spanish? – A little.

check.q: In Mexiko spricht man ____.
check.why: The language ends in -isch, has a capital and takes no article after sprechen. Spanien is the country.

tips.title: Nationalities are nouns, and take -in for women
tips.text: der Engländer / die Engländerin, der Spanier / die Spanierin, der Franzose / die Französin, der Türke / die Türkin. Deutsche is special: ein Deutscher / eine Deutsche. No article after sein: Ich bin Österreicherin.

examples.de: Er ist Italiener und sie ist Italienerin.
examples.en: He is Italian and she is Italian.

examples.de: Ich bin Deutsche.
examples.en: I am German (said by a woman).

check.q: Marie kommt aus Frankreich. Sie ist ____.
check.why: A woman from France is eine Französin (der Franzose is the man), and after sein there is no article. Französisch is the language.

tips.title: Norden, Süden, Osten, Westen
tips.text: The four directions are der-nouns and take im: im Norden, im Süden, im Osten, im Westen. Hamburg liegt im Norden von Deutschland; Von Deutschland aus liegt Polen im Osten. Two directions join into one word: im Südwesten, im Nordosten.

examples.de: Hamburg liegt im Norden von Deutschland.
examples.en: Hamburg is in the north of Germany.

examples.de: Von Deutschland aus liegt Polen im Osten.
examples.en: Seen from Germany, Poland lies to the east.

examples.de: Spanien liegt im Südwesten.
examples.en: Spain lies to the south-west.

tips.trap: The nouns are capitalised and keep -en: im Norden, not im Nord.

check.q: München liegt im ____ von Deutschland.
check.why: Munich is in Bavaria, the south of Germany.

remember: Four countries wear an article: die Schweiz, die Türkei, die USA, die Niederlande — 'the Swiss, the Turks, the Americans, the Dutch'.
Languages end in -isch and start with a capital: Englisch, Spanisch, Türkisch.
im Norden · im Süden · im Osten · im Westen — der-nouns, always with im.

context.de: Hallo! Ich bin Yusuf und komme aus der Türkei. Ich spreche Türkisch, Englisch und jetzt auch ein bisschen Deutsch. Meine Frau ist Polin – sie kommt aus Krakau. Unsere Nachbarn sind Amerikaner, sie kommen aus den USA. Und woher kommst du?
context.en: Hi! I'm Yusuf and I come from Turkey. I speak Turkish, English and now a little German too. My wife is Polish – she comes from Kraków. Our neighbours are American, they come from the USA. And where are you from?

mistakes.why: die Schweiz keeps its article, and after aus it becomes der.
The language is a noun and takes a capital.
Nationalities after sein take no article.

help.hook: Where are you from, what do you speak, what are you — the three questions every new German conversation starts with.

Sprache — Man spricht …: {subject}: what language do people speak there?
{subject}: many people there speak that language.
Nationalität — Er ist …: {subject}: he is a man from there (his nationality).
{subject}: my father is a man from there (his nationality).
Nationalität — Sie ist …: {subject}: she is a woman from there (her nationality).
{subject}: my mother is a woman from there (her nationality).
Himmelsrichtung — von Deutschland aus: Seen from Germany, {subject} lies to the … (north, south, east, west?)

help.intro: Saying where you are is something you do every day — Ich bin im Büro, wir sind in der Stadt, sie ist bei ihren Eltern — and a small set of prepositions covers it: in, an, auf, bei, aus, von, vor, unter (and nach for Wohin?, which has its own quiz in the next module). Behind them sits the dative case, which changes der to dem and die to der, and glues in + dem into im and an + dem into am. You will learn the dative as a system later in the course. For now you learn these as fixed chunks, the way a child does: im Park, am Bahnhof, in der Schule, bei Siemens, beim Arzt. The pairing is what matters: in for inside or in a town or country, an for at (a station, the sea, the university), bei for at a person’s or a company’s, auf / vor / unter for on, in front of and under something, and for ‘from’ the mirror image — aus for out of a place, von for from a person, a company or a point.

tips.title: im / in der / in — inside, or in a place
tips.text: in + der-/das-word → im (im Park, im Büro, im Kino); in + die-word → in der (in der Schule, in der Stadt); towns and most countries: in Berlin, in Deutschland.

examples.de: Ich bin im Büro. Anna ist in der Schule.
examples.en: I am at the office. Anna is at school.

examples.de: Wir wohnen in Deutschland, in Köln.
examples.en: We live in Germany, in Cologne.

check.q: Mein Bruder ist ____ Kino.
check.why: das Kino is a das-word, so in + dem melts into im: im Kino, like im Büro.

tips.title: am / bei / beim — at
tips.text: am for a point or place you are at but not inside: am Bahnhof, am Meer, an der Uni. bei for a person's home or a company: bei meinen Eltern, bei Siemens, beim Arzt (bei + dem).

examples.de: Ich warte am Bahnhof.
examples.en: I'm waiting at the station.

examples.de: Er arbeitet bei Siemens. Sie ist beim Arzt.
examples.en: He works at Siemens. She's at the doctor's.

check.q: Heute Abend esse ich ____ meiner Oma.
check.why: At a person's home is bei: bei meiner Oma, bei meinen Eltern.

tips.title: aus / vom / von — from
tips.text: aus = out of a place you were inside (aus dem Büro, aus der Schule, aus Italien); von = from a person, a company, or an activity (von meinen Eltern, von Siemens, vom Arzt, von der Arbeit).

examples.de: Ich komme gerade aus dem Supermarkt.
examples.en: I've just come from the supermarket.

examples.de: Sie kommt vom Arzt.
examples.en: She's coming from the doctor's.

tips.trap: the article after these prepositions is dative: dem, der, den. English 'in the' never changes; German 'in dem' becomes 'im'. Learn the chunk, not the rule, for now.

check.q: Ich komme gerade ____ Zahnarzt.
check.why: From a person is von, not aus (you were never inside the dentist), and von + dem becomes vom.

tips.title: auf / vor / unter — on, in front of, under
tips.text: For where a thing is: auf dem Tisch (on the table), vor dem Haus (in front of the house), unter dem Tisch (under the table). The dem after them is the same dative chunk as in im and am.

examples.de: Das Buch liegt auf dem Tisch.
examples.en: The book is lying on the table.

examples.de: Das Auto steht vor dem Haus.
examples.en: The car is in front of the house.

check.q: The cat is sleeping under the bed: Die Katze schläft ____ dem Bett.
check.why: unter = under, auf = on, vor = in front of — each followed by the same dem chunk.

tips.title: im–am–beim: the three contractions
tips.text: in dem → im, an dem → am, bei dem → beim, von dem → vom. Whenever you hear a preposition ending in -m, it has swallowed a dem.

examples.de: im Bett, am Fenster, beim Bäcker, vom Bahnhof
examples.en: in bed, at the window, at the baker's, from the station

examples.de: Ich bin im Büro. Sie ist beim Arzt.
examples.en: I'm at the office. She's at the doctor's.

check.q: Which words are hidden inside beim?
check.why: A preposition ending in -m has swallowed a dem: bei dem → beim, like in dem → im.

remember: im = inside a der/das place · in der = inside a die place · am = at · bei = at someone's.
Mirror pairs: in ↔ aus (inside ↔ out of), bei ↔ von (at someone's ↔ from someone).

context.de: Wo bist du? – Ich bin noch im Büro. Und du? – Ich bin in der Stadt, am Bahnhof. Ich komme gerade vom Arzt. – Und Lena? – Sie ist bei ihren Eltern in Hamburg. Sie kommt morgen aus Hamburg zurück.
context.en: Where are you? – I'm still at the office. And you? – I'm in town, at the station. I've just come from the doctor's. – And Lena? – She's at her parents' in Hamburg. She's coming back from Hamburg tomorrow.

mistakes.why: in + dem is always contracted to im in speech and normal writing.
At a company or a person's place is bei, not in.
Origin from a country or city is aus; von is for people and points.

help.hook: Im Büro, am Bahnhof, beim Arzt — learn where-you-are as ready-made chunks and you can say where you are all day.

sentences.sentence: Wo bist du? – Ich bin ____ . (der Park)
sentences.english: Where are you? – I am in the park.
sentences.why: Being somewhere (wo?) takes in + dative: der Park → dem Park, and in dem shrinks to im.

sentences.sentence: Wo ist Anna? – Sie ist ____ . (der Bahnhof)
sentences.english: Where is Anna? – She is at the station.
sentences.why: At a point like the station it is an + dative: an dem → am Bahnhof.

sentences.sentence: Wo ist Tom? – Er ist ____ . (der Supermarkt)
sentences.english: Where is Tom? – He is at the supermarket.
sentences.why: Inside a building: in + dative; der Supermarkt → dem, and in dem = im.

sentences.sentence: Wo sind die Kinder? – Sie sind ____ . (die Schule)
sentences.english: Where are the children? – They are at school.
sentences.why: die-words take der in the dative: in der Schule.

sentences.sentence: Wo seid ihr? – Wir sind ____ . (die Stadt)
sentences.english: Where are you? – We are in town.
sentences.why: wo? means dative, and die Stadt becomes der Stadt: in der Stadt.

sentences.sentence: Wo ist Mama? – Sie ist ____ . (die Küche)
sentences.english: Where is Mum? – She is in the kitchen.
sentences.why: die Küche in the dative is der Küche: in der Küche.

sentences.sentence: Wo ist Lisa? – Sie ist ____ . (die Uni)
sentences.english: Where is Lisa? – She is at the university.
sentences.why: Institutions like the Uni take an + dative: an der Uni.

sentences.sentence: Wo bist du? – Ich bin noch ____ . (das Büro)
sentences.english: Where are you? – I am still at the office.
sentences.why: das-words take dem in the dative, and in dem shrinks to im: im Büro.

sentences.sentence: Wo sind Anna und Tom? – Sie sind ____ . (das Kino)
sentences.english: Where are Anna and Tom? – They are at the cinema.
sentences.why: das Kino → dem Kino; in dem = im Kino.

sentences.sentence: Wo ist das Kind? – Es ist schon ____ . (das Bett)
sentences.english: Where is the child? – It is already in bed.
sentences.why: Lying in bed is a place (wo?): in + dative — im Bett.

sentences.sentence: Wo wohnt ihr? – Wir wohnen ____ . (Deutschland)
sentences.english: Where do you live? – We live in Germany.
sentences.why: Country names without an article take plain in: in Deutschland.

sentences.sentence: Wo arbeitest du? – Ich arbeite ____ . (die Bank)
sentences.english: Where do you work? – I work at the bank.
sentences.why: Working at an employer is bei + dative: bei der Bank.

sentences.sentence: Wo ist Lena? – Sie ist ____ . (meine Eltern)
sentences.english: Where is Lena? – She is at my parents’.
sentences.why: At a person's place it is bei + dative; plural dative adds -n: bei meinen Eltern.

sentences.sentence: Wo ist Herr Braun? – Er ist ____ . (der Arzt)
sentences.english: Where is Mr Braun? – He is at the doctor’s.
sentences.why: At a person (the doctor's) it is bei + dative: bei dem → beim Arzt.

sentences.sentence: Woher kommst du? – Ich komme ____ . (der Park)
sentences.english: Where are you coming from? – I am coming from the park.
sentences.why: Coming from somewhere (woher?) is aus or von + dative: aus dem Park.

sentences.sentence: Woher kommt Anna? – Sie kommt ____ . (der Bahnhof)
sentences.english: Where is Anna coming from? – She is coming from the station.
sentences.why: From a point you were at (am Bahnhof) you come vom — von dem — Bahnhof.

sentences.sentence: Woher kommt ihr? – Wir kommen ____ . (der Supermarkt)
sentences.english: Where are you coming from? – We are coming from the supermarket.
sentences.why: Out of a building is aus + dative: aus dem Supermarkt.

sentences.sentence: Woher kommen die Kinder? – Sie kommen ____ . (die Schule)
sentences.english: Where are the children coming from? – They are coming from school.
sentences.why: woher? takes dative: die Schule → der Schule — aus der Schule.

sentences.sentence: Woher kommt Lisa? – Sie kommt ____ . (die Uni)
sentences.english: Where is Lisa coming from? – She is coming from the university.
sentences.why: From the Uni (where you are an der Uni) you come von der Uni — dative die → der.

sentences.sentence: Woher kommst du? – Ich komme ____ . (das Büro)
sentences.english: Where are you coming from? – I am coming from the office.
sentences.why: Out of the building: aus + dative — das Büro → dem, aus dem Büro.

sentences.sentence: Woher kommt er? – Er kommt ____ . (Berlin)
sentences.english: Where is he from? – He is from Berlin.
sentences.why: Towns and countries without an article take plain aus: aus Berlin.

sentences.sentence: Woher kommt der Brief? – Er kommt ____ . (die Bank)
sentences.english: Where is the letter from? – It is from the bank.
sentences.why: A letter comes from a sender: von + dative — von der Bank.

sentences.sentence: Woher kommt Herr Braun? – Er kommt ____ . (der Arzt)
sentences.english: Where is Mr Braun coming from? – He is coming from the doctor’s.
sentences.why: From a person's place it is von + dative: von dem → vom Arzt — the pair of beim Arzt.

sentences.sentence: Woher kommt das Paket? – Es kommt ____ . (meine Eltern)
sentences.english: Where is the parcel from? – It is from my parents.
sentences.why: A parcel from people: von + dative, and the plural dative adds -n — von meinen Eltern.

sentences.sentence: Das Buch liegt ____ dem Tisch. (on)
sentences.english: The book is lying on the table.
sentences.why: auf is 'on top of'; lying somewhere is a position (wo?), so dative follows: auf dem Tisch.

sentences.sentence: Der Hund schläft ____ dem Tisch. (under)
sentences.english: The dog is sleeping under the table.
sentences.why: unter is 'under'; the dog stays put, so dative: unter dem Tisch.

sentences.sentence: Das Auto steht ____ dem Haus. (in front of)
sentences.english: The car is standing in front of the house.
sentences.why: vor is 'in front of'; the car is parked (wo?), so dative: vor dem Haus.

sentences.sentence: Woher kommt Mama? – Sie kommt ____ . (die Küche)
sentences.english: Where is Mum coming from? – She is coming from the kitchen.
sentences.why: Out of a room: aus + dative — aus der Küche.

sentences.sentence: Woher kommt ihr? – Wir kommen ____ . (Deutschland)
sentences.english: Where are you from? – We are from Germany.
sentences.why: Origin from a country without an article: plain aus — aus Deutschland.

sentences.sentence: Die Katze schläft ____ dem Bett. (under)
sentences.english: The cat is sleeping under the bed.
sentences.why: unter = 'under'; sleeping is staying in place, so dative follows: unter dem Bett.

sentences.sentence: Das Handy liegt ____ dem Bett. (on)
sentences.english: The phone is lying on the bed.
sentences.why: auf = 'on'; the phone just lies there (wo?), so dative: auf dem Bett.

help.intro: German builds words the way it builds numbers: by gluing pieces together. The two pieces to start with are the ending -in, which turns a male person-word into the female one (der Lehrer → die Lehrerin, der Student → die Studentin), and the compound noun, which fuses two nouns into one — die Schokolade + der Kuchen = der Schokoladenkuchen, das Haus + die Tür = die Haustür. Both let you understand far more than you have learnt: once you know Kuchen, you know Apfelkuchen, Käsekuchen and Geburtstagskuchen. Two rules cover nearly everything: -in is always die, with plural -innen and sometimes an umlaut (Arzt → Ärztin, Koch → Köchin); and a compound takes the gender of its last part. The umlaut in Ärztin and Köchin is checked strictly (type ae/oe if you have no umlaut keys).

tips.title: -in makes it female, -innen makes them plural
tips.text: Lehrer → Lehrerin → Lehrerinnen. Always die. Some add an umlaut: Arzt → Ärztin, Koch → Köchin, Franzose → Französin. -e words drop the e: Kollege → Kollegin, Pole → Polin.

examples.de: Meine Ärztin ist sehr nett.
examples.en: My (female) doctor is very nice.

examples.de: Die Kolleginnen kommen aus Polen.
examples.en: The (female) colleagues come from Poland.

check.q: Mein Vater ist Koch und meine Mutter ist auch ____.
check.why: -in makes the female form, and Koch adds an umlaut on the way: der Koch → die Köchin.

tips.title: Compounds: the last word rules
tips.text: die Schokolade + der Kuchen = der Schokoladenkuchen (der, because Kuchen is der). das Haus + die Tür = die Haustür. The first word describes; the last word says what it is and gives the gender.

examples.de: der Apfelkuchen, die Fischsuppe, das Kinderzimmer
examples.en: apple cake (der Kuchen), fish soup (die Suppe), children's room (das Zimmer)

examples.de: das Haus + die Tür = die Haustür
examples.en: house + door = front door (die, from Tür)

tips.trap: English 'apple cake' is two words with no gender; German fuses them and the gender comes from cake, not apple.

check.q: ____ Gartentür ist offen. (der Garten + die Tür)
check.why: The last part gives the gender: Tür is die, so it is die Gartentür, even though Garten is der.

visual.caption: The last piece gives the article and the main meaning.

tips.title: The little joint: -s-, -n-, -e-
tips.text: Some compounds add a linking letter: Geburtstag + Kuchen = Geburtstagskuchen (-s-), Schokolade + Kuchen = Schokoladenkuchen (-n-). You will absorb these by reading; nobody learns them as rules.

examples.de: der Geburtstagskuchen, der Schokoladenkuchen
examples.en: birthday cake, chocolate cake

examples.de: der Hund + die Hütte = die Hundehütte
examples.en: dog + hut = kennel (-e-)

check.q: der Geburtstag + die Party = die ____
check.why: Geburtstag always takes the little -s- joint when it glues onto another word, just like Geburtstagskuchen.

tips.title: Read compounds from the back
tips.text: Kinderzimmer: Zimmer (room) … for Kinder (children). Haustür: Tür (door) … of the Haus. Start at the end and the word explains itself.

examples.de: das Wohnzimmer, das Schlafzimmer, das Badezimmer
examples.en: living room, bedroom, bathroom — all Zimmer, all das

examples.de: die Haustür: Tür … vom Haus
examples.en: front door: a door … of the house

check.q: Read it from the back: what is ein Kinderbuch?
check.why: The last part says what it is — Buch, a book — and the first part says what kind: for Kinder.

remember: -in = she, -innen = they (all women), and both are die.
In a compound, the last word is the boss: it gives the meaning and the gender.

context.de: In meiner Firma arbeiten viele Frauen: meine Chefin, zwei Kolleginnen aus Italien und eine Journalistin. In der Kantine gibt es heute Fischsuppe und Apfelkuchen. Der Apfelkuchen ist von der Köchin – sehr lecker!
context.en: Lots of women work at my company: my boss, two colleagues from Italy and a journalist. In the canteen today there's fish soup and apple cake. The apple cake is from the cook – delicious!

mistakes.why: Short vowels a/o often take an umlaut in the -in form.
A final -e is dropped before -in.
The compound takes the gender of its last part, der Kuchen.

help.hook: German glues words together like building blocks — learn the pieces and Apfelkuchen, Haustür and Lehrerin explain themselves.

sentences.sentence: Herr Kern ist Lehrer. Frau Kern ist auch ____ . (der Lehrer)
sentences.english: Mr Kern is a teacher. Mrs Kern is a teacher too.
sentences.why: -in turns a male job word female: der Lehrer → die Lehrerin.

sentences.sentence: Paul ist Student und Maria ist ____ . (der Student)
sentences.english: Paul is a student and Maria is a student.
sentences.why: Add -in for the woman: der Student → die Studentin.

sentences.sentence: Tom ist mein Freund und Anna ist meine ____ . (der Freund)
sentences.english: Tom is my friend and Anna is my friend.
sentences.why: der Freund + -in = die Freundin — the -in makes it female.

sentences.sentence: Herr Wolf ist Arzt. Seine Frau ist auch ____ . (der Arzt)
sentences.english: Mr Wolf is a doctor. His wife is a doctor too.
sentences.why: -in, and the vowel often takes an umlaut: der Arzt → die Ärztin.

sentences.sentence: Im Café arbeiten ein Kellner und eine ____ . (der Kellner)
sentences.english: A waiter and a waitress work in the café.
sentences.why: der Kellner + -in = die Kellnerin — the waitress.

sentences.sentence: Max ist Schüler und Lena ist ____ . (der Schüler)
sentences.english: Max is a pupil and Lena is a pupil.
sentences.why: der Schüler + -in = die Schülerin.

sentences.sentence: Im Supermarkt fragt Anna eine ____ . (der Verkäufer)
sentences.english: In the supermarket Anna asks a shop assistant.
sentences.why: der Verkäufer + -in = die Verkäuferin — the shop assistant.

sentences.sentence: Herr Berg ist Koch. Frau Berg ist auch ____ . (der Koch)
sentences.english: Mr Berg is a cook. Mrs Berg is a cook too.
sentences.why: -in plus umlaut: der Koch → die Köchin.

sentences.sentence: Frau Klein wohnt neben mir. Sie ist meine ____ . (der Nachbar)
sentences.english: Mrs Klein lives next to me. She is my neighbour.
sentences.why: der Nachbar + -in = die Nachbarin — no umlaut here.

sentences.sentence: Anna arbeitet mit mir. Sie ist meine ____ . (der Kollege)
sentences.english: Anna works with me. She is my colleague.
sentences.why: An -e man-word drops the -e before -in: der Kollege → die Kollegin.

sentences.sentence: Sabine schreibt für die Zeitung. Sie ist ____ . (der Journalist)
sentences.english: Sabine writes for the newspaper. She is a journalist.
sentences.why: der Journalist + -in = die Journalistin.

sentences.sentence: John ist Amerikaner und Mary ist ____ . (der Amerikaner)
sentences.english: John is American and Mary is American.
sentences.why: Nationalities work the same way: der Amerikaner → die Amerikanerin.

sentences.sentence: An der Schule arbeiten viele ____ . (der Lehrer → Frauen, Plural)
sentences.english: Many female teachers work at the school.
sentences.why: The plural of an -in word doubles the n: Lehrerin → Lehrerinnen.

sentences.sentence: In Köln wohnen viele ____ . (der Student → Frauen, Plural)
sentences.english: Many female students live in Cologne.
sentences.why: -in → -innen in the plural: Studentinnen.

sentences.sentence: Anna hat drei ____ . (der Freund → Frauen, Plural)
sentences.english: Anna has three female friends.
sentences.why: Freundin + -nen = Freundinnen — every -in plural ends in -innen.

sentences.sentence: Meine zwei ____ kommen aus Italien. (der Kollege → Frauen, Plural)
sentences.english: My two female colleagues come from Italy.
sentences.why: Kollegin → Kolleginnen: the -in plural always doubles the n.

sentences.sentence: Im Krankenhaus arbeiten viele ____ . (der Arzt → Frauen, Plural)
sentences.english: Many female doctors work in the hospital.
sentences.why: Ärztin → Ärztinnen — umlaut from the feminine, -innen for the plural.

sentences.sentence: Die ____ im Supermarkt sind nett. (der Verkäufer → Frauen, Plural)
sentences.english: The female shop assistants in the supermarket are nice.
sentences.why: Verkäuferin → Verkäuferinnen: -in doubles its n in the plural.

sentences.sentence: die Schokolade + der Kuchen = der ____
sentences.english: chocolate + cake = chocolate cake
sentences.why: In a compound the last word rules: a Kuchen of Schokolade is der Schokoladenkuchen — Schokolade links with -n.

sentences.sentence: das Haus + die Tür = die ____
sentences.english: house + door = front door
sentences.why: The last word decides the article: die Tür makes it die Haustür, whatever Haus is.

sentences.sentence: der Apfel + der Kuchen = der ____
sentences.english: apple + cake = apple cake
sentences.why: Apfel + Kuchen join directly, nothing in between: der Apfelkuchen.

sentences.sentence: die Kinder + das Zimmer = das ____
sentences.english: children + room = children’s room
sentences.why: The last word rules: das Zimmer → das Kinderzimmer, the room for the children.

sentences.sentence: der Fisch + die Suppe = die ____
sentences.english: fish + soup = fish soup
sentences.why: die Suppe is last, so the soup wins: die Fischsuppe.

sentences.sentence: der Geburtstag + der Kuchen = der ____
sentences.english: birthday + cake = birthday cake
sentences.why: Geburtstag links with an -s: der Geburtstagskuchen — the s glues many compounds.

sentences.sentence: Im Haus wohnen zwei nette ____ . (der Nachbar → Frauen, Plural)
sentences.english: Two nice female neighbours live in the building.
sentences.why: Nachbarin → Nachbarinnen — the -in plural doubles the n.

sentences.sentence: Im Restaurant kochen heute zwei ____ . (der Koch → Frauen, Plural)
sentences.english: Two female cooks are cooking in the restaurant today.
sentences.why: Köchin → Köchinnen: umlaut from the feminine, -innen for the plural.

sentences.sentence: die Woche + das Ende = das ____
sentences.english: week + end = weekend
sentences.why: das Ende is last and rules the article; Woche links with -n: das Wochenende.

sentences.sentence: die Arbeit + der Platz = der ____
sentences.english: work + place = workplace
sentences.why: der Platz is last, so der Arbeitsplatz — Arbeit takes the linking -s.

sentences.sentence: der Hund + das Futter = das ____
sentences.english: dog + food = dog food
sentences.why: das Futter rules the article; Hund links with -e: das Hundefutter.

quizzes.title: Gespräch: Das bin ich

help.intro: The closing conversation of this module, run in your own AI assistant with voice mode on: a seven-minute chat about you — name, where you live and come from, your family, and the numbers and colours around you. Copy the exercise, paste it in, say 'Los geht's', and answer in full sentences. The tutor will not interrupt to correct you; it keeps every correction for the report at the end, together with a score you bring back here. This is as close to a real first conversation as practice gets: someone asking, you answering in whole sentences, with the verb endings and sein/haben forms carrying the meaning.

tips.title: Answer the question that was asked, in a full sentence
tips.text: Woher kommst du? → Ich komme aus … (not 'Aus Spanien'). Wie alt bist du? → Ich bin … Jahre alt. Match the verb in the question.

examples.de: Hast du Geschwister? – Ja, ich habe einen Bruder.
examples.en: Do you have siblings? – Yes, I have a brother.

examples.de: Wo wohnst du? – Ich wohne in Lyon.
examples.en: Where do you live? – I live in Lyon.

check.q: Woher kommst du? Pick the full-sentence answer to this question.
check.why: The question uses kommst, so you answer with the matching ich komme aus … in a full sentence.

tips.title: Use what this level gave you
tips.text: sein and haben, the -e / -st / -t endings, der/die/das, numbers to 100, colours: the tutor listens for exactly these.

examples.de: Mein Auto ist blau. Ich habe zwei Katzen. Sie sind schwarz.
examples.en: My car is blue. I have two cats. They are black.

examples.de: Mein Bruder ist zwanzig und wohnt in Wien.
examples.en: My brother is twenty and lives in Vienna.

check.q: Meine Katzen ____ weiß.
check.why: Meine Katzen are 'they', and sein for sie (plural) is sind.

tips.title: Ask back
tips.text: Und du? / Und Sie? turns an answer into a conversation and buys you a second to think.

examples.de: Ich komme aus Irland. Und du?
examples.en: I'm from Ireland. And you?

examples.de: Ich habe zwei Geschwister. Und Sie?
examples.en: I have two siblings. And you?

check.q: Ich heiße Mia. ____ du?
check.why: Und du? hands the question back: 'And you?'

remember: Whole sentences only — the score is on the sentence, not the word.
Keep talking through mistakes; the corrections come at the end.
help.exam: A short conversation about yourself and your family is the heart of the A1 speaking exam — and of every first chat with a neighbour.
help.hook: Hold a five-minute chat about yourself in German: your name, home, family, and the numbers and colours around you.

speaking.topic: Introducing myself: my name, where I live, where I come from, my family, numbers and colours around me.
practisePoints: Present-tense endings: ich heiße, du heißt, er wohnt
sein and haben: ich bin, ich habe
Answering W-Fragen: Wie? Wo? Woher? Wie alt?
Colours and numbers around me: Mein Auto ist rot. Ich habe zwei Brüder.
scoringCriteria: the verb ending for the person
sein/haben forms
answering the question that was asked
the colour or number itself
priorityErrors: wrong verb ending
wrong form of sein or haben
answering a different question

quizzes.imageDescription: a young woman student waving in front of a university building with a coffee cup, a small brother and sister beside her

writing.topic: Introduce yourself in writing, the way you would on a profile or a form: your name, how old you are, where you come from, where you live now, what you do, and one thing you like.
practisePoints: say your name with heißen or sein
say where you come from with kommen aus and where you live with wohnen in
say your age with sein
write every noun with a capital letter
keep the verb in second place in each sentence
scoringCriteria: all six pieces of information are there
each piece is a full sentence, not a form entry (Name: Anna)
the text is about me, in the first person

help.hook: Write six true sentences about yourself, and have them corrected one by one.
help.intro: Your first piece of real German writing. Six short sentences are enough: your name, your age, where you are from, where you live, what you do, and one thing you like. You write them here in the box, and the app builds a correction request that carries your own text to your AI, which corrects what you actually wrote. Aim for 120 to 300 characters. Do not reach for words you have not met yet. A short, correct text scores better than an ambitious one full of guesses, and that is true at every level of this course.

tips.title: The verb is always the second idea
tips.text: German puts the conjugated verb in second position, whatever comes first. If you open with the subject, the verb follows it. If you open with something else, the verb still comes second and the subject moves behind it.

examples.de: Ich wohne jetzt in Berlin.
examples.en: I live in Berlin now.

examples.de: Jetzt wohne ich in Berlin.
examples.en: Now I live in Berlin.

check.q: Heute ____ ich Deutsch.
check.why: After an opening word the verb comes straight away, then the subject.

tips.trap: „Jetzt ich wohne in Berlin“ is the commonest first mistake: the verb has been pushed to third place.

tips.title: heißen, sein, kommen, wohnen
tips.text: Four verbs carry a self-introduction. ich heiße (I am called), ich bin (I am), ich komme aus (I come from), ich wohne in (I live in). aus is for the country or town you are from; in is for where you live now.

examples.de: Ich heiße Ana und ich bin 26 Jahre alt.
examples.en: My name is Ana and I am 26.

examples.de: Ich komme aus Spanien und wohne in Hamburg.
examples.en: I am from Spain and live in Hamburg.

check.q: Ich komme ____ Italien.
check.why: aus is the preposition for the country you come from.

tips.title: Every noun gets a capital letter
tips.text: German writes every noun with a capital letter, wherever it stands in the sentence: Jahre, Spanien, Deutsch, Familie, Bruder. It is the thing a corrector notices first in a written text, and it costs nothing to get right.

examples.de: Ich lerne Deutsch und ich habe einen Bruder.
examples.en: I am learning German and I have a brother.

examples.de: Meine Familie wohnt in Madrid.
examples.en: My family lives in Madrid.

check.q: Which is written correctly?
check.why: Schwester is a noun, so it is capitalised, and the sentence starts with a capital too.

remember: The verb is the second idea, always.
ich heiße, ich bin, ich komme aus, ich wohne in.
Every noun takes a capital letter.
Six true sentences beat twelve guessed ones.
help.exam: Writing a few lines about yourself is the first written task of the A1 certificate, and the first thing anyone asks you in German.

mistakes.why: The verb keeps second place; the subject moves behind it.
aus for the country you come from.
German has an age with sein, not haben.
The name of a language is a noun.

vocab.en: gladly, used to say you like doing something

help.intro: Wie schreibt man das? — how do you spell that? — is a question you will hear on your first day in any German office, and on the phone, at the doctor's and at every hotel desk you will be asked to spell your name. The German alphabet has the same 26 letters as English plus ä, ö, ü and ß, but many letters have different names, and the ones that differ are exactly the ones English speakers mix up: E is said 'ay' and I is said 'ee' (the other way round from what you expect), J is Jot, V is Vau (said 'fow'), W is We (said 'vay'), Z is Zett ('tset') and Y is Ypsilon. Germans spell with a few fixed helpers: Doppel-L for ll, A-Umlaut for ä, Eszett or scharfes S for ß. This quiz asks for the names of the tricky letters, then gives you names spelt out letter by letter and asks you to write the word.

tips.title: E is "ay", I is "ee"
tips.text: The two vowels English speakers swap: E sounds like English 'ay' in 'day', I like 'ee' in 'see'. A is 'ah', O is 'oh', U is 'oo'.

examples.de: Wie heißen Sie? – Meier. Em – E – I – E – Er.
examples.en: What's your name? – Meier. M – 'ay' – 'ee' – 'ay' – R.

examples.de: Lisa: El – I – Es – A.
examples.en: Lisa: L – 'ee' – S – 'ah'.

tips.trap: When a German spells 'E – I' you hear 'ay – ee'. Write E first, then I.

check.q: Someone spelling a word says 'ee'. Which letter is it?
check.why: In German the letter I sounds like English 'ee', while E sounds like 'ay'.

tips.title: The letters with surprising names
tips.text: J = Jot, V = Vau, W = We, Y = Ypsilon, Z = Zett, Q = Ku, C = Ce (said "tsay"), H = Ha. Say them aloud until they are as automatic as A, B, C.

examples.de: Jot – A – En: Jan
examples.en: J – A – N: Jan

examples.de: Vau – A – Te – E – Er: Vater
examples.en: V – A – T – E – R: Vater

check.q: What is the German name of the letter W?
check.why: W is We (said 'vay'). Vau is the name of V, and Doppel-U is not used.

tips.title: Spelling helpers
tips.text: Two identical letters: Doppel- (Doppel-L, Doppel-S). Umlauts: A-Umlaut, O-Umlaut, U-Umlaut. ß: Eszett or scharfes S. Capital or small: groß / klein.

examples.de: Müller: Em – U-Umlaut – Doppel-El – E – Er.
examples.en: Müller: M – Ü – double L – E – R.

examples.de: Straße schreibt man mit Eszett.
examples.en: Straße is written with ß.

check.q: What do you call ß when you spell a word?
check.why: ß is Eszett (or scharfes S). Doppel-S means two separate s letters, as in Wasser.

tips.title: The front-desk script
tips.text: Wie ist Ihr Name? – … Können Sie das bitte buchstabieren? – Gern: … Practise your own name and your street until you can spell them without stopping.

examples.de: Können Sie das bitte buchstabieren?
examples.en: Could you spell that, please?

examples.de: Wie schreibt man das? – Mit Ha am Ende.
examples.en: How do you write that? – With an H at the end.

check.q: You want a name spelt out letter by letter: Können Sie das bitte ____?
check.why: buchstabieren means to spell aloud, letter by letter (from Buchstabe, letter).

remember: E = 'ay', I = 'ee' — the swap that causes most spelling mistakes.
J Jot, V Vau, W We, Z Zett: four letters, four names to learn by heart.

context.de: Wie ist Ihr Name, bitte? – Weber. – Können Sie das buchstabieren? – We – E – Be – E – Er. – Danke. Und Ihr Vorname? – Jana: Jot – A – En – A.
context.en: What's your name, please? – Weber. – Could you spell that? – W – E – B – E – R. – Thanks. And your first name? – Jana: J – A – N – A.

mistakes.wrong: Meier spelt 'M – I – E – I – R'
mistakes.why: E is said 'ay' and I 'ee' — English speakers hear 'ee' and write I.
German W is We; the sound is also how the letter is said in words: Wien, Wasser.
German Z is always ts — in its name too.

help.hook: Wie schreibt man das? Master the dozen letter names that differ from English and you can spell your name anywhere.

sentences.sentence: Der Buchstabe J heißt auf Deutsch ____ .
sentences.english: The letter J is called ____ in German.
sentences.why: J is called Jot — said like 'yot'; a German j always sounds like English y.

sentences.sentence: Der Buchstabe V heißt auf Deutsch ____ .
sentences.english: The letter V is called ____ in German.
sentences.why: V is called Vau — said 'fow'; in German words v usually sounds like f.

sentences.sentence: Der Buchstabe W heißt auf Deutsch ____ .
sentences.english: The letter W is called ____ in German.
sentences.why: W is called We — said 'vay'; German w sounds like English v.

sentences.sentence: Der Buchstabe Z heißt auf Deutsch ____ .
sentences.english: The letter Z is called ____ in German.
sentences.why: Z is called Zett — and sounds like 'ts', as in Zeit.

sentences.sentence: Der Buchstabe Y heißt auf Deutsch ____ .
sentences.english: The letter Y is called ____ in German.
sentences.why: Y keeps its Greek name: Ypsilon.

sentences.sentence: Der Buchstabe H heißt auf Deutsch ____ .
sentences.english: The letter H is called ____ in German.
sentences.why: H is called Ha — just 'hah', not 'aitch'.

sentences.sentence: Der Buchstabe Q heißt auf Deutsch ____ .
sentences.english: The letter Q is called ____ in German.
sentences.why: Q is called Ku — said like 'koo', the cow word Kuh sounds the same.

sentences.sentence: Straße schreibt man mit ß. Dieser Buchstabe heißt ____ .
sentences.english: Straße is written with ß. This letter is called ____.
sentences.why: ß is the Eszett ('s-z'), also called scharfes S — it always sounds like a sharp double s.

sentences.sentence: Käse schreibt man mit ä. Dieser Buchstabe heißt ____ .
sentences.english: Käse is written with ä. This letter is called ____.
sentences.why: ä is spelt out as A-Umlaut — Umlaut names the two dots that change the vowel's sound.

sentences.sentence: Ich buchstabiere: Ha – A – En – Es. Mein Vorname ist ____ .
sentences.english: I spell: H – A – N – S. My first name is ____.
sentences.why: Read each letter's name back: Ha=H, A, En=N, Es=S — Hans.

sentences.sentence: Jot – U – El – I – A. Mein Vorname ist ____ .
sentences.english: J – U – L – I – A. My first name is ____.
sentences.why: Jot=J, then U-L-I-A — Julia; remember Jot is the J.

sentences.sentence: We – I – E – En. Die Stadt heißt ____ .
sentences.english: W – I – E – N. The city is called ____.
sentences.why: We=W, I, E, En=N — Wien, Vienna; We is the letter W, said 'vay'.

sentences.sentence: Vau – A – Te – E – Er. Das Wort ist ____ .
sentences.english: V – A – T – E – R. The word is ____.
sentences.why: Vau=V, A, Te=T, E, Er=R — Vater; Vau is the letter V.

sentences.sentence: Zett – E – Ha – En. Die Zahl ist ____ .
sentences.english: Z – E – H – N. The number is ____.
sentences.why: Zett=Z, E, Ha=H, En=N — zehn, the number ten.

sentences.sentence: Em – E – I – E – Er. Der Nachname ist ____ .
sentences.english: M – E – I – E – R. The surname is ____.
sentences.why: Em=M, E, I, E, Er=R — Meier; ei is said like English 'eye'.

sentences.sentence: Be – E – Er – El – I – En. Die Stadt heißt ____ .
sentences.english: B – E – R – L – I – N. The city is called ____.
sentences.why: Be=B, E, Er=R, El=L, I, En=N — Berlin.

sentences.sentence: Ka – A – Te – Zett – E. Das Tier ist eine ____ .
sentences.english: K – A – T – Z – E. The animal is a ____.
sentences.why: Ka=K, A, Te=T, Zett=Z, E — Katze; Zett is the z.

sentences.sentence: Em – U-Umlaut – Doppel-El – E – Er. Der Nachname ist ____ .
sentences.english: M – Ü – double L – E – R. The surname is ____.
sentences.why: U-Umlaut is ü, Doppel-El a double l: M-ü-ll-e-r — Müller.

help.intro: Rents, prices of bikes and phones, distances, the year you were born: from here on the numbers get long, and German writes them as one word — 650 is sechshundertfünfzig, 1.200 is tausendzweihundert. The good news is that nothing new is hidden inside them. You say the hundreds, then the last two digits exactly as you learnt them, with the unit first: 385 = dreihundert-fünfundachtzig. Thousands work the same way: 8.500 = achttausend-fünfhundert. Two things are different from English. First, German marks thousands with a full stop and decimals with a comma: 1.200 means twelve hundred, 1,20 means one point two. Second, years before 2000 are said in hundreds: 1998 is neunzehnhundertachtundneunzig, never 'tausendneunhundert…'; from 2000 on you say zweitausend: 2020 = zweitausendzwanzig.

tips.title: Hundreds + the number you already know
tips.text: Say how many hundreds, then the last two digits the German way (unit + und + ten). All of it is one word; ein before hundert and tausend is optional.

examples.de: Die Wohnung kostet sechshundertfünfzig Euro.
examples.en: The flat costs 650 euros.

examples.de: Das Buch hat vierhundertsechzehn Seiten.
examples.en: The book has 416 pages.

tips.trap: Do not insert spaces or an extra und after hundert: sechshundertfünfzig, not "sechshundert und fünfzig".

check.q: Das Regal kostet ____ Euro. (230)
check.why: Say the hundreds, then the last two digits, all as one word with no extra und after hundert.

tips.title: Thousands: the full stop is not a decimal point
tips.text: 1.200 = tausendzweihundert (also zwölfhundert). 8.500 = achttausendfünfhundert. 20.000 = zwanzigtausend. A comma is the decimal point: 1,5 Kilo = one and a half kilos.

examples.de: Die Halle hat tausendzweihundert Plätze.
examples.en: The hall has 1,200 seats.

examples.de: Die Stadt hat zwanzigtausend Einwohner.
examples.en: The town has 20,000 inhabitants.

tips.trap: In English 1.200 is 'one point two'. In German it is twelve hundred.

check.q: A German sign says: 2.500 Einwohner. How many people live there?
check.why: In German the full stop marks thousands: 2.500 = zweitausendfünfhundert. The decimal point is a comma.

tips.title: Years: hundreds before 2000, zweitausend after
tips.text: 1965 = neunzehnhundertfünfundsechzig. 1998 = neunzehnhundertachtundneunzig. 2020 = zweitausendzwanzig. And a year stands alone: Ich bin 1998 geboren — no in.

examples.de: Mein Vater ist neunzehnhundertfünfundsechzig geboren.
examples.en: My father was born in 1965.

examples.de: Meine Tochter ist zweitausendzwanzig geboren.
examples.en: My daughter was born in 2020.

check.q: Meine Mutter ist ____ geboren. (1972)
check.why: Years before 2000 are said in hundreds (neunzehnhundert…), and the year stands alone without in.

tips.title: Read from the left, flip the last two
tips.text: Take 585: fünfhundert (left) + fünfundachtzig (flip the 8 and the 5). Only the last pair is ever flipped.

examples.de: 585 → fünfhundert + fünfundachtzig
199 → hundert + neunundneunzig

check.q: Which one is 376?
check.why: Read the hundreds from the left (dreihundert), then flip only the last pair: 76 = sechsundsiebzig.

tips.title: Ordinal numbers: -te up to 19, -ste from 20
tips.text: Dates and rankings use ordinals, written with a full stop: der 1. Mai = der erste Mai. Add -te to the numbers 2 to 19 (zweite, vierte, zehnte, neunzehnte) and -ste from 20 upwards (zwanzigste, dreißigste, hundertste). Three are irregular: erste, dritte, siebte.

examples.de: Heute ist der erste Mai.
examples.en: Today is the first of May.

examples.de: Morgen ist der dritte Juni.
examples.en: Tomorrow is the third of June.

examples.de: Der einunddreißigste Dezember ist Silvester.
examples.en: The thirty-first of December is New Year’s Eve.

tips.trap: The full stop after the figure is the ordinal mark: 3. Juni reads dritte Juni, never drei Juni.

check.q: Heute ist der ____ Oktober. (20.)
check.why: From 20 on the ending is -ste.

remember: One number, one word: sechshundertfünfzig, tausendzweihundert.
Years before 2000 in hundreds (neunzehnhundert…), after 2000 with zweitausend.
Ordinals: -te to 19, -ste from 20; erste, dritte, siebte are irregular. 3. Juni = dritte Juni.

context.de: Die Wohnung hat zwei Zimmer und kostet neunhundertachtzig Euro im Monat. Das Haus ist alt – es ist von neunzehnhundertzwölf. Bis zur Arbeit sind es nur zwölf Kilometer, und das Fahrrad kostet hundertneunundneunzig Euro.
context.en: The flat has two rooms and costs 980 euros a month. The house is old – it is from 1912. It is only twelve kilometres to work, and the bike costs 199 euros.

mistakes.why: The whole number is one word, and there is no und after hundert.
Years before 2000 are said in hundreds.
The full stop groups thousands; the comma is the decimal point.

help.hook: Rent, bikes, birth years: big German numbers are just the small ones you know, glued into one long word.

sentences.sentence: Die Wohnung kostet ____ Euro im Monat. (650)
sentences.english: The flat costs 650 euros a month.
sentences.why: Hundreds stack up front: sechs·hundert, then fünfzig — all one word, no 'and' after the hundred.

sentences.sentence: Das Fahrrad kostet ____ Euro. (199)
sentences.english: The bike costs 199 euros.
sentences.why: hundert, then units before tens: neun·und·neunzig — 'nine-and-ninety'.

sentences.sentence: Unsere Schule hat ____ Schüler. (300)
sentences.english: Our school has 300 pupils.
sentences.why: A round hundred is just the digit + hundert: dreihundert.

sentences.sentence: Mein Zimmer im Hotel hat die Nummer ____ . (112)
sentences.english: My hotel room has the number 112.
sentences.why: hundert + zwölf — 13 to 19 and the teens keep their own words, so no swapping here.

sentences.sentence: Von Berlin nach München sind es ____ Kilometer. (585)
sentences.english: It is 585 kilometres from Berlin to Munich.
sentences.why: fünfhundert, then units first: fünf·und·achtzig — 'five-and-eighty'.

sentences.sentence: Das Buch hat ____ Seiten. (416)
sentences.english: The book has 416 pages.
sentences.why: vierhundert + sechzehn — sechzehn is a teen word, said as is (and it clips sechs to sech-).

sentences.sentence: Die Miete ist ____ Euro. (980)
sentences.english: The rent is 980 euros.
sentences.why: neunhundert + achtzig — a plain ten needs no swap: achtzig.

sentences.sentence: Der Deutschkurs kostet ____ Euro. (120)
sentences.english: The German course costs 120 euros.
sentences.why: hundert + zwanzig; the ein- in front of hundert is optional.

sentences.sentence: Der Zug fährt ____ Kilometer pro Stunde. (250)
sentences.english: The train goes 250 kilometres an hour.
sentences.why: zweihundert + fünfzig — hundreds first, then the rest, one word.

sentences.sentence: Die Halle hat ____ Plätze. (1.200)
sentences.english: The hall has 1,200 seats.
sentences.why: tausend + zweihundert; German can also say zwölfhundert, 'twelve hundred'.

sentences.sentence: Das Auto kostet ____ Euro. (8.500)
sentences.english: The car costs 8,500 euros.
sentences.why: acht·tausend·fünf·hundert — thousands, then hundreds, all one word.

sentences.sentence: Die Stadt hat ____ Einwohner. (20.000)
sentences.english: The town has 20,000 inhabitants.
sentences.why: zwanzig·tausend — say the 20, then tausend; big numbers chain the same way.

sentences.sentence: Ich bin ____ geboren. (1998)
sentences.english: I was born in 1998.
sentences.why: Years before 2000 are said in hundreds: neunzehn·hundert + achtundneunzig — 'nineteen hundred…'.

sentences.sentence: Mein Vater ist ____ geboren. (1965)
sentences.english: My father was born in 1965.
sentences.why: neunzehnhundert + fünf·und·sechzig — hundreds for the year, units before tens.

sentences.sentence: Meine Tochter ist ____ geboren. (2020)
sentences.english: My daughter was born in 2020.
sentences.why: From 2000 on, years are plain numbers: zweitausend·zwanzig — no hundreds trick.

sentences.sentence: Die Reise kostet ____ Euro. (2.400)
sentences.english: The trip costs 2,400 euros.
sentences.why: zweitausendvierhundert — or vierundzwanzighundert, 'twenty-four hundred', like in English.

sentences.sentence: Mein Opa ist ____ geboren. (1937)
sentences.english: My grandpa was born in 1937.
sentences.why: neunzehnhundert + sieben·und·dreißig — the year in hundreds, units before tens.

sentences.sentence: Der Fernseher kostet ____ Euro. (1.399)
sentences.english: The TV costs 1,399 euros.
sentences.why: tausend·dreihundert + neunundneunzig — units before tens close the number.

sentences.sentence: Ich wohne seit ____ in Köln. (2008)
sentences.english: I have lived in Cologne since 2008.
sentences.why: Years from 2000 are plain: zweitausend·acht.

sentences.sentence: Heute ist der ____ Mai. (1.)
sentences.english: Today is the first of May.
sentences.why: Dates take ordinals; 'first' is irregular: der erste — not einte.

sentences.sentence: Morgen ist der ____ Juni. (3.)
sentences.english: Tomorrow is the third of June.
sentences.why: 'Third' is irregular: der dritte — not dreite.

sentences.sentence: Der ____ Tag der Woche ist der Sonntag. (7.)
sentences.english: The seventh day of the week is Sunday.
sentences.why: Ordinals to 19 add -te; sieben clips to siebte.

sentences.sentence: Heute ist der ____ Oktober. (20.)
sentences.english: Today is the twentieth of October.
sentences.why: From 20 up, ordinals add -ste: der zwanzigste.

sentences.sentence: Der ____ Dezember ist Silvester. (31.)
sentences.english: The thirty-first of December is New Year’s Eve.
sentences.why: einunddreißig + -ste = der einunddreißigste — big ordinals take -ste.

cards.en: would like (ich möchte = I would like)
gladly, used to say you like doing something

help.intro: Every word this module's exercises use, on one deck of flashcards: the nouns from the article and plural drills, the numbers, the family, the colours, the countries and the verbs. A noun is learnt with its article or not at all, so the write mode only counts "die Stelle", never "Stelle" on its own. Three ways to work through the deck: write the German, choose it from four options, or flip the card and rate yourself honestly. A word you miss comes back later in the same run, and stays in your "Weak words" list until you get it right three times in a row.

tips.title: Article first, always
tips.text: German nouns come in three genders and the article is the only reliable clue. Say der Tisch, die Lampe, das Buch as one word each; a bare noun is only half a word.

examples.de: der Tisch, die Tische
examples.en: the table, the tables

examples.de: die Lampe, die Lampen
examples.en: the lamp, the lamps

examples.de: das Buch, die Bücher
examples.en: the book, the books

check.q: You are learning the word for “chair”. What should you memorise?
check.why: The article is the only reliable clue to the gender, so the noun and its article are learnt as one word.

visual.caption: Say the article every time you say the word, and it sticks.

tips.title: Learn the plural with the noun
tips.text: The plural is shown after every correct answer. Read it aloud once: the pattern (-e, -en, -s, -er, umlaut) is what you are memorising, not just the word.

examples.de: der Apfel, die Äpfel
examples.en: the apple, the apples

examples.de: das Kind, die Kinder
examples.en: the child, the children

check.q: der Stuhl, die ____
check.why: Stuhl takes the umlaut + -e pattern: die Stühle. Saying the plural aloud with the noun is how the pattern sticks.

tips.title: Names take no article
tips.text: Countries, cities and letters are capitalised like nouns but stand alone: Berlin, Spanien, Japan. The exceptions with an article are die Schweiz, die Türkei, die USA.

examples.de: Ich komme aus Spanien.
examples.en: I come from Spain.

examples.de: Ich komme aus der Schweiz.
examples.en: I come from Switzerland.

check.q: Mein Freund kommt aus ____.
check.why: Country and city names stand alone without an article; only a few like die Schweiz and die Türkei keep one.

remember: Never say a noun without its article — not even in your head.
Miss a word? It comes back in the same run. Get it right three times and it leaves the weak list.
help.hook: A German noun without its article is only half a word — learn der, die or das and the plural with it, every time.

quizzes.title: Suchbild: Das Wohnzimmer
quizzes.sceneAlt: A cosy living room: a window with a curtain, a floor lamp, a guitar and an armchair on the left, a picture, a clock and wall shelves with a vase, a radio and a telephone on the back wall, a television on a cabinet, a sofa with a cat, a coffee table on a round rug, a dog and a ball on the floor, and by the door an umbrella, a plant and a basket of wool.

help.hook: A cosy living room full of everyday things: tap each one in the picture, then give it its article.
help.intro: A picture hunt instead of a deck: one cosy, slightly cluttered living room with 32 things to find in it, the everyday words you need first — der Tisch, die Lampe, das Sofa, the cat asleep on the cushions and the dog on the rug. The prompt asks Wo ist der Sessel? and you tap it in the picture. Each find shows its label, coloured by its gender, then leaves a small tick in that colour, so you can see what you have already found. Once you have passed a run, the hunt turns harder: the prompt hides the article (Wo ist ___ Sessel?), and after the find you choose der, die or das yourself. A tap on bare wall costs nothing; a tap on the wrong object tells you what you hit and you keep looking, and after three misses the right one is shown. No object is asked twice in the same run.

tips.title: Many nouns in -e are die
tips.text: Look at how many words in this room end in -e: die Lampe, die Tasse, die Kerze, die Vase, die Katze, die Pflanze, die Gitarre. Most German nouns ending in -e are feminine, so when you meet a new one, guess die first.

examples.de: die Kerze, Plural: -n
examples.en: candle

examples.de: die Gitarre, Plural: -n
examples.en: guitar

check.q: ____ Tasse steht auf dem Tisch.
check.why: Tasse ends in -e, and most nouns in -e are feminine: die Tasse.

tips.title: Die Brille is one thing
tips.text: English says glasses, a plural, but German says die Brille, one object. And das Glas is something else: the glass of water on the table. Don’t mix them up.

examples.de: die Brille
examples.en: (a pair of) glasses

examples.de: das Glas, Plural: Gläser
examples.en: drinking glass

check.q: Which one do you put on your nose?
check.why: Die Brille is the pair of glasses; das Glas is for drinking.

tips.title: International words in -o or -a are often das
tips.text: Words German took from other languages and that end in -o or -a are usually neuter: das Sofa, das Radio, das Auto. Picture them all parked together in one das-garage.

examples.de: das Sofa, Plural: -s
examples.en: sofa

examples.de: das Radio, Plural: -s
examples.en: radio

check.q: ‘the toy car’ in German:
check.why: Auto ends in -o, like Radio: das Auto.

remember: Most nouns ending in -e are die: die Lampe, die Tasse, die Katze.
Die Brille is singular in German: one pair of glasses.
A compound takes the article of its last part: der Regen + der Schirm → der Regenschirm.

quizzes.title: Suchbild: Das Klassenzimmer
quizzes.sceneAlt: An empty classroom: a chalkboard, a world map and a coat hook with a jacket on the back wall, a sink, a towel, a fish tank and a stool on the left, a piano with a woolly hat on the right, a teacher’s desk with a computer, a globe and a printer, and in front a school desk covered with an exercise book, paper, a ruler, a pencil, a pencil case, scissors, a calculator, a lunch box, a banana and a bottle.

help.hook: An empty classroom after the bell: tap each thing you find, then give it its article.
help.intro: A picture hunt instead of a deck: one empty, slightly messy classroom with 32 things to find in it, the words of a school day — die Tafel, der Bleistift, das Heft, the fish tank by the wall and the piano in the corner. The prompt asks Wo ist das Lineal? and you tap it in the picture. Each find shows its label, coloured by its gender, then leaves a small tick in that colour, so you can see what you have already found. Once you have passed a run, the hunt turns harder: the prompt hides the article (Wo ist ___ Lineal?), and after the find you choose der, die or das yourself. A tap on bare wall costs nothing; a tap on the wrong object tells you what you hit and you keep looking, and after three misses the right one is shown. No object is asked twice in the same run.

tips.title: Compounds in the classroom: the last part decides
tips.text: Many classroom words are two words glued together, and the last part decides the article. Papier + Korb: der Korb, so der Papierkorb. Land + Karte: die Karte, so die Landkarte. Hand + Tuch: das Tuch, so das Handtuch.

examples.de: der Bleistift, Plural: -e
examples.en: pencil (der Stift)

examples.de: die Brotdose, Plural: -n
examples.en: lunch box (die Dose)

check.q: ____ Waschbecken ist links an der Wand.
check.why: The last part is das Becken, so the whole word is das Waschbecken.

tips.title: Machines in -er are der
tips.text: A thing that does a job and ends in -er is usually masculine: der Computer, der Drucker, der Taschenrechner. The -er here is not a plural, it is part of the word.

examples.de: der Drucker, Plural: -
examples.en: printer

examples.de: der Taschenrechner, Plural: -
examples.en: calculator

check.q: Which article goes with Computer?
check.why: Computer ends in -er like Drucker: der Computer.

tips.title: -chen is always das
tips.text: A noun ending in -chen is always neuter, whatever it means: das Mäppchen, the little pencil case. Think of -chen as a small green das sticker on anything little.

examples.de: das Mäppchen, Plural: -
examples.en: pencil case

examples.de: das Brötchen, Plural: -
examples.en: bread roll

check.q: ____ Mäppchen liegt auf der Schulbank.
check.why: Every noun ending in -chen is neuter: das Mäppchen.

remember: The last part of a compound sets the article: der Korb → der Papierkorb.
Machines in -er are der: der Computer, der Drucker.
-chen is always das: das Mäppchen.

help.intro: German marks the job a noun does in the sentence by changing its article — that is what a 'case' is. The nominative is the subject (the one doing); the accusative is the direct object (the one it is done to): Der Mann sieht den Hund — the man sees the dog. This is the first case beyond the nominative, and the friendliest: only the masculine changes. der becomes den, ein becomes einen; feminine, neuter and plural look exactly as they did. Every transitive verb — haben, sehen, kaufen, essen, brauchen, möchten — takes an accusative object, so you will use this in nearly every sentence from now on. Ask 'wen oder was?' (whom or what?) after the verb and the answer is the accusative.

tips.title: Only masculine moves: der → den, ein → einen
tips.text: Feminine (die / eine), neuter (das / ein) and plural (die) are identical in nominative and accusative. All the work is in the masculine column.

examples.de: Ich sehe den Mann. Ich habe einen Hund.
examples.en: I see the man. I have a dog.

examples.de: Ich sehe die Frau, das Kind und die Kinder.
examples.en: I see the woman, the child and the children. (no change)

tips.trap: English shows the object by word order alone. German shows it on the article, and later on adjectives and pronouns too. This is the start of the case system.

check.q: Ich sehe ____ Lehrerin. (die Lehrerin)
check.why: Only masculine nouns change in the accusative. Lehrerin is a die-word, so the article stays die.

visual.caption: One cell changes in the whole accusative: the masculine. Everything else stays as it was.

tips.title: wen oder was? — ask the verb
tips.text: The accusative answers 'whom or what?' after the verb: Ich kaufe (was?) einen Apfel. Ich kenne (wen?) den Lehrer. If the question is 'wer?' (who is doing it), that is the nominative.

examples.de: Wer kauft? – Der Mann. Was kauft er? – Einen Apfel.
examples.en: Who is buying? – The man (nom.). What is he buying? – An apple (acc.).

examples.de: Wen siehst du? – Den Lehrer.
examples.en: Whom do you see? – The teacher.

check.q: ____ trinkt den Kaffee? – Der Mann.
check.why: The question asks who is doing the drinking, the subject, so it takes the nominative wer. wen asks for the object.

rows.en: Same meaning: the article, not the order, says who sees whom.

tips.title: The verbs that always take it
tips.text: haben, brauchen, kaufen, sehen, essen, trinken, lesen, suchen, finden, möchten, kennen, es gibt — the object after them is accusative. Note es gibt: Es gibt einen Park.

examples.de: Ich brauche einen Stift. Hast du einen Moment?
examples.en: I need a pen. Do you have a moment?

examples.de: Es gibt hier einen Supermarkt.
examples.en: There is a supermarket here.

check.q: Es gibt hier ____ Bahnhof. (der Bahnhof)
check.why: es gibt always takes the accusative, and Bahnhof is masculine: ein → einen.

tips.title: -n on the blue words
tips.text: The masculine is the blue column in every table here. In the accusative the blue words grow an -n: den, einen, keinen, meinen. Red, green and plural stay put.

examples.de: der Hund → den Hund · ein Hund → einen Hund
examples.en: blue grows an n

examples.de: kein Stift → keinen Stift · mein Bruder → meinen Bruder
examples.en: no pen · my brother — the masculine object adds -en

check.q: Ich besuche ____ Bruder. (my, der Bruder)
check.why: Bruder is masculine and the object of besuchen, so mein grows an -en: meinen Bruder.

remember: Only the masculine changes, and it just adds -(e)n: den, einen, keinen, meinen.
wer? = nominative, wen? = accusative — ask the question, get the case.

context.de: Ich gehe einkaufen. Ich brauche einen Apfel, eine Banane und ein Brot. Im Supermarkt sehe ich den Nachbarn. Er kauft einen Kaffee und die Zeitung. Dann sehe ich das Auto von meinem Chef – und meinen Chef!
context.en: I'm going shopping. I need an apple, a banana and a loaf. In the supermarket I see the neighbour. He buys a coffee and the paper. Then I see my boss's car – and my boss!

mistakes.why: Hund is masculine; as an object it takes einen.
Neuter never changes in the accusative.
The object of sehen is accusative: der → den.

help.hook: German shows who does what with the article, and in the accusative only der-words change: der Hund becomes den Hund.

help.intro: Possessive articles say whose something is — mein, dein, sein, ihr, unser, euer, Ihr — and they behave exactly like ein: they take the ein-endings, decided by the noun that follows, not by the owner. So mein Vater (masculine), mein Kind (neuter), meine Mutter (feminine), meine Eltern (plural); and in the accusative the masculine adds -en: Ich sehe meinen Vater. The owner only decides which word you start from: sein for his (and for its with a der/das-word), ihr for her (and for their), Ihr with a capital for your (formal). Choose the owner, then add the ending for the noun — two separate decisions, in that order.

tips.title: Pick the owner
tips.text: ich → mein · du → dein · er/es → sein · sie (she) → ihr · wir → unser · ihr (you all) → euer · sie (they) → ihr · Sie → Ihr.

examples.de: Das ist Tom. Sein Auto ist neu.
examples.en: That's Tom. His car is new.

examples.de: Das ist Anna. Ihr Auto ist alt.
examples.en: That's Anna. Her car is old.

check.q: Ben und ich lernen Deutsch. ____ Lehrer heißt Herr Wolf. (Our teacher …)
check.why: The owners are wir (Ben and I), and wir → unser. euer belongs to ihr (you all).

tips.title: Then add the ein-ending for the noun
tips.text: Nominative: no ending for masculine and neuter (mein Vater, mein Kind); -e for feminine and plural (meine Mutter, meine Kinder). Accusative: masculine adds -en (meinen Vater), the rest as in the nominative.

examples.de: Meine Schwester heißt Mia. Ich sehe meine Schwester.
examples.en: My sister is called Mia. I see my sister. (feminine: same both times)

examples.de: Mein Bruder ist hier. Ich sehe meinen Bruder.
examples.en: My brother is here. I see my brother. (masculine: -en as object)

check.q: Ich suche ____ Schlüssel. (der Schlüssel, my key)
check.why: Schlüssel is masculine and the object of suchen, so it takes -en, exactly like einen.

visual.caption: The ending comes from the noun, exactly as with ein.

tips.title: sein vs ihr — his vs her
tips.text: sein looks like 'sie' but means his; ihr means her (and their). Decide by the owner's gender, never by the noun's: Anna und ihr Bruder; Tom und seine Schwester.

examples.de: Anna und ihr Hund. Tom und sein Hund.
examples.en: Anna and her dog. Tom and his dog.

examples.de: Die Kinder und ihre Eltern.
examples.en: The children and their parents.

tips.trap: 'sein' ≠ 'sie'. English speakers map sein → she; it is the opposite: sein = his.

check.q: Herr Becker ruft ____ Tochter an. (his daughter)
check.why: The owner is a man, so his = sein; Tochter is feminine, so it gets -e: seine Tochter.

visual.caption: The owner decides sein or ihr; the noun decides the ending.

tips.title: euer loses an e
tips.text: With an ending, euer drops its second e: eure Mutter, euren Vater, eure Kinder. unser keeps everything: unsere Mutter.

examples.de: Wo ist eure Lehrerin? Ist das euer Haus?
examples.en: Where is your (pl.) teacher? Is that your house?

examples.de: Wir besuchen euren Vater und eure Kinder.
examples.en: We're visiting your father and your children.

check.q: Kinder, wo sind ____ Schuhe?
check.why: Schuhe is plural, so the possessive takes -e, and euer drops its second e: eure.

remember: Owner first, noun second: 'sein/ihr' comes from the owner, the ending comes from the noun.
A possessive is an ein-word — whatever ein does, mein does too.

context.de: Das ist meine Familie. Mein Vater arbeitet in Bonn, meine Mutter ist Ärztin. Meine Schwester hat einen Hund – ihr Hund heißt Bello. Mein Bruder hat eine Katze; seine Katze ist schwarz. Und unser Haus? Es ist klein, aber wir lieben unser Haus.
context.en: This is my family. My father works in Bonn, my mother is a doctor. My sister has a dog – her dog is called Bello. My brother has a cat; his cat is black. And our house? It's small, but we love our house.

mistakes.why: The owner is female, so her = ihr; sein is his.
Masculine object takes -en, exactly like einen.
Neuter takes no ending in the nominative and accusative.

help.hook: Say whose things are whose — mein, dein, sein, ihr — and get the ending right by looking at the noun, not the owner.

quizzes.title: Hören: Im Café

help.intro: A guest orders in a café: cake first, then a drink, then the bill — all of it only heard. Two people speaking is the new difficulty, so each line of the transcript starts with the speaker (Kellner, Gast). The waiter asks and names the price; the guest answers and pays. Keep a mental list as you listen: what is ordered, what is offered but refused, what it costs, what is paid. The ordering verbs are your signposts: nehmen and möchten (what is ordered), Was macht das? and Das macht … (the price). Listen once to get the two voices apart, then once for each question. The phrases here — Was möchten Sie? Ich nehme … Das macht … Stimmt so — are the script you will use yourself at every café table.

tips.title: The signpost verbs
tips.text: nehmen and möchten introduce what is ordered; Was macht das? / Das macht … introduces the price. Wait for those words and the answers come to you.

examples.de: Ich nehme ein Stück Apfelkuchen, bitte.
examples.en: I'll have a piece of apple cake, please.

examples.de: Das macht vier Euro achtzig.
examples.en: That comes to 4.80 €.

check.q: 'Ich möchte einen Tee. – Gern. … Das macht drei Euro zehn.' What does the tea cost?
check.why: Das macht introduces the price: drei Euro zehn is 3.10 €.

tips.title: Two voices: who asks, who answers
tips.text: The waiter asks with Sie (Möchten Sie …?) and states the price; the guest answers with ich. What is ordered is in the guest's lines; the price is in the waiter's.

examples.de: Kellner: Möchten Sie den Kaffee mit Milch?
examples.en: Waiter: Would you like the coffee with milk?

examples.de: Gast: Ja, gern, mit Milch und Zucker.
examples.en: Guest: Yes please, with milk and sugar.

check.q: Which line belongs to the guest?
check.why: The guest speaks with ich and orders; the waiter asks with Sie and names the price.

tips.title: Offered is not ordered
tips.text: When the waiter offers something and the guest says 'Nein, danke', it is not part of the order. The question will try to catch you with it.

examples.de: Möchten Sie auch ein Glas Wasser? – Nein, danke, nur den Kaffee.
examples.en: Would you like a glass of water too? – No thanks, just the coffee.

examples.de: Hier sind fünf Euro. Stimmt so.
examples.en: Here are five euros. Keep the change.

check.q: 'Möchten Sie auch einen Salat? – Nein, danke. Ich nehme nur die Suppe.' What does the guest order?
check.why: Nein, danke takes the salad off the order, so only the soup is ordered.

remember: Guest = what; waiter = how much. Listen for each in its own voice.
'Nein, danke' removes an item from the order; 'Stimmt so' means keep the change.
help.exam: Ordering, refusing and paying in a café is a standard short dialogue in the A1 exam — and your first real conversation in any German-speaking town.
help.hook: Follow a café order between waiter and guest and catch what is ordered, what is refused and what it all costs.
